title: Customer network troubleshooting log — Jun 09 2026
content:
Context:
We ran a 4-hour troubleshooting block with Customer X (Emea region) on 2026-06-09 after their GPU workers started failing TLS handshakes and intermittent model-loading errors following a change to their on-prem edge NAT gateway. Symptoms appeared ~2026-06-08 22:00 UTC after the customer applied a firmware upgrade to the gateway and rotated the SNAT address pool.

Attendees:
- Customer X: network lead (Omar), platform lead (Sofia), SRE (Raj)
- Redwood: Aisha (lead), Luca (network), Priya (k8s/runtime), Tom (telemetry), Marta (solutions)

Summary of observed failures:
- TLS handshake timeouts from worker nodes to Redwood private controlplane (10–30% of requests) — TLS errors were ERR_SSL_PROTOCOL_ERR / premature close.
- Frequent EFS/NFS mount refresh failures during model loads: log shows "stale file handle" and repeated remount attempts, causing model server cold-starts to fail and rollout to quickly revert.
- kubelet conversations showed spikes in conntrack table usage on the NAT gateway (customer reported conntrack hit-counts at 70–90% of capacity immediately after gateway rotation).
- Intermittent DNS resolution failures for internal controlplane endpoints — short 5–20s windows where A record resolution returned NXDOMAIN; TTLs are 60s.

Hypothesis and root-cause indicators:
- Gateway firmware change altered conntrack timeout defaults (TCP_ESTABLISHED reduced) and aggressive SNAT reuse, which combined with our high-churn short-TCP connections (lots of small TLS connections from runtime) caused premature connection tracking evictions and reset behavior. Evicted conntrack entries -> server sees connections as new -> TLS session resumption broken -> handshake failures.
- NFS errors are likely downstream of file-handle invalidation when nodes are behind NAT with asymmetric routing; when conntrack evicts, subsequent mounts surface stale handles because the NFS server sees a different 5-tuple.
- DNS issues look correlated to a management-plane load spike; possiblity that customer’s internal DNS forwarders hit rate limits during gateway SNAT churn.

What we tried during the session (live changes):
1) Increased conntrack max and extended timeouts on customer's NAT gateway (temporary knob). Immediate drop in conntrack evictions observed in gateway metrics.
2) Switched a canary subset of node traffic to use a static SNAT pool (reduced SNAT churn). TLS handshake error rate on canary nodes dropped to <1%.
3) Bumped kube-proxy conntrack settings on affected nodes (net/netfilter parameters) and restarted kube-proxy. Improved pod-to-controlplane stability for that node group.
4) Flushed DNS cache and increased DNS forwarder worker count, temporarily stabilized NXDOMAIN incidents.
5) Replayed model-loads after remounts; NFS errors reduced but not eliminated for nodes that had asymmetric pathing.

Decisions made / temporary mitigations:
- Customer will retain increased conntrack table and timeouts as a short-term mitigation for 72 hours.
- Redwood to roll a small runtime patch that prefers TLS connection reuse (keep-alive) and reduces short-lived connection churn for the next rollout — target: 2026-06-12 canary. This is a mitigative measure, not a full fix.
- Do not change production TTLs until we validate DNS forwarder load plan.

Action items (owners + deadlines):
- Luca: Produce a small runbook for customer firewall/NAT knobs we changed (list exact sysctls and conntrack keys). Due: 2026-06-10.
- Priya: Prepare a runtime canary build that increases TCP keepalive (SO_KEEPALIVE + tuned intervals) and enables connection pooling in the model loader library. Add feature flag. Due: 2026-06-11.
- Aisha & Marta: Draft a customer-facing summary (what happened, what we changed, recommended long-term fixes) and schedule a 30-min follow-up with Customer X stakeholders. Due: 2026-06-10.
- Tom: Correlate telemetry around TLS handshake failures with conntrack evictions across last 72 hours; provide a one-pager heatmap. Due: 2026-06-10.
- Customer (Omar + Raj): Provide gateway firmware exact changelog and SNAT pool config; also confirm whether HA path asymmetry was introduced by the firmware. Due: 2026-06-10.

Open questions / risks:
- Is the firmware change intentional for conntrack behavior? If yes, customer needs to negotiate vendor config; if not, they may want to roll back.
- Long-term: we should assess whether our runtime should default to longer-lived connections in private deployments behind NATs — this has cost and resource implications (more persistent TCP sockets).
- Edge case: if customer scales to larger concurrent connections, conntrack growth could still be a recurring operational burden; consider advising on a dedicated egress appliance or static SNAT ranges per node pool.

Suggested long-term remediation (engineering proposals):
- Work with customer to provision static SNAT IPs per node pool (or per rack) so source 5-tuples remain stable.
- Implement a runtime capability: adaptive connection pooling (increase pool size for private deployments when behind NAT). Feature should be flag-gated and evaluated for memory/socket overhead.
- Add conntrack-aware health checks in our installer: detect when gateway conntrack is near capacity and surface warnings during install/handoff.
- Add NFS mount idempotency workaround for asymmetric NAT (fall back to a persistence proxy or use SMB/managed block storage if possible).

Notes for handoff to install team:
- This is higher-severity than typical: customer production throughput impacted for some traffic patterns. We should update our Private Deployments install checklist to include: 
  * Verify egress conntrack limits and recommend defaults
  * Recommend DNS forwarder sizing and health checks
  * Document SNAT strategy options (static IPs, per-node pools)

Immediate follow-up meeting:
- 2026-06-11 14:00 UTC — 30m follow-up with Customer X. Agenda: confirm firmware details, review runtime canary plan, agree rollback window if failures recur.

Appendix (logs / diagnostic commands used during session):
- netstat -s | grep conntrack (showed large TCP timeout count)
- conntrack -L | wc -l (conntrack entries peaked ~280k; gateway limit 320k)
- journalctl -u kubelet | grep "stale file handle"
- tcpdump -i eth0 host <controlplane-ip> and filter "tcp[tcpflags] & (tcp-syn|tcp-fin) != 0" (captured SYNs without SYN-ACKs during high-churn windows)

If anything obvious missing from notes or anyone wants to add raw snippets, paste them below and we’ll stitch into the playbook.

-- Aisha
